##### **High prices, but higher risk (part 2)** 

We concluded in last month’s report with the comment “Given the current elevated base metal prices, GFMS believes that a constant stream of bullish news is required to support these levels.  We do not believe that this “news flow “will be maintained and we are cautious about the prospects for further price increases”.  Obviously this bullish news flow did dry up and the GFMS Base Metal Index fell from a recent peak of 401.47 on April to 345.61 on May 6.  Howev

er, as has been the case in this cycle, corrections are generally short-lived as they are seen by many as buying opportunities with the index quickly regaining the 360 level. 

###### **More volatility is on the way** 

Just prior to the publication of this report, there was another correction in the market.  This was triggered by both slower than expected industrial production growth and higher than expected inflation in China.  Sentiment will not be helped by the Chinese central bank to raise the banks’ reserve requirements by a further 0.5 percentage points effective May 18, the fifth such move in recent times.  Such developments then sees the markets’ focus return to earlier data releases such as the decline in Chinese copper imports in April (see Copper section for details). 

The performance of the individual metals in the recent rout largely reflected earlier price moves rather the specific underlying fundamentals.  The decline in aluminium prices of 6.2% was the lowest while the recent peak-to-trough fall for tin was the largest.  While this variable performance is not unexpected in any short term correction, the fundamental position of the metals should reassert itself in terms of relative pricing. 

The trigger for the move would appear to be concerns about the rate of economic growth, particularly in China.  While growth rates within the country will remain high the fear is that attempts to rein in inflation and curb the property bubble will lead to a slowdown in the rate of expansion. Another trigger was the strengthening of the dollar, which might better be described as a weakening of the euro.  The return of the issue of sovereign debt (not that it ever really went away) added to the mix.  There are also concerns about what the post Quantitative Easing two (QE2) environment will look like.  If there is not a QE3 then interest rates will rise, which would put further pressure on the commodity complex.  Apart from funds switching their asset allocation to reflect this move, a higher interest rate environment could see some of long-term warehousing deals unravel. 

###### **Demand environment is unchanged for now** 

Given the exceptionally high prices both from a historical context, and in relation to the marginal costs of production, markets are always vulnerable to a correction.  However at this stage most of the demand indicators remain positive.  In the Economics section, we look at some of the forward-looking economic indicators, which in most cases are pointing to continued growth.  Although data on nonferrous semis shipments and downstream steel shipments are lagging rather than leading indicators, apart from the earthquake related dip in Japan, most of these statistics suggest that demand is holding up well.  This view is reinforced by the anecdotal evidence that we receive and by the increases in physical premiums.  We believe that a reasonably strong demand backdrop will help limit the downside. The March result implies that the disaster in Japan and the souring energy prices had not impacted much on the manufacturing sector over the month. The United States consumer confidence index, a more forward looking indicator, which has been registering falls in recent months also staged a rebound in April. However, we note that the Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) in the country fell by 0.8 points over the month. Nevertheless, this should not generate any concerns, considering that the level has been well above the historical average of 52.7 year to date. China’s economy remained robust, although there have been signs of easing growth. Industrial production increased by 13.4% year-on-year in April, decelerating from the nearly 15% year-on-year increase achieved in both February and March. The slightly lower growth largely reflects monetary tightening policies, the phasing out of fiscal measures, and overcapacity in certain sectors. Nonetheless, China’s GDP continued to grow strongly by 9.7% year-on-year over the first quarter, coupled with gains in fixed asset investment. Unsurprisingly, Japan’s industrial production growth fell by a massive 15.3% month-on-month in March due to the earthquake and tsunami that hit part of the country on March 11th. Problems including damage to factories, power outages and supply disruptions will likely continue to crimp production in the near term. In line with this, Japanese consumer confidence also saw a sharp decline in March. Furthermore, interruptions in the supply chain have also affected industrial output in Japan’s key export markets. Notably, automakers in the United States and Canada may have to cut output in the second quarter due to a shortage of parts from Japan. **A1** Independent - Informed - International Aluminium - May 2011 ###### **Market background** Although not immune from the correction in industrial commodities, aluminium has outperformed the rest of the base metal sector. In the recent sell-off (early May) aluminium prices fell by 6.2% compared to a 12.4% decline in the GFMS Base Metal Index (BMI). Again the relatively strong performance has come about with little fundamental support. We note, for example, the contrast between the latest production figures for aluminium and copper. The former shows output setting a new high, while the latter registered a decline in April. Investment activity continues to be supportive for aluminium as funds look for relative value in the sector. Secondly, a lot of the massive LME stockpile is not available to the market given long-term warehousing deals, which has contributed to the rise in physical premiums. ###### **Stock levels largely unchanged** Since our previous r

eport LME inventories have been fairly stable and are around 4.6 million tonnes in mid May, over 300,000 tonnes higher than at the start of the year. Stocks of unwrought aluminium held by producers as reported by the International Aluminium Association (IAI) have also trended higher so far this year, rising by 153,000 tonnes in the first three months to 1.549 million tonnes. The increase has largely been down to North America. The region saw inventories climb by 128,000 tonnes to 355,000 tonnes. This reflects the sharp increase to production (see below for details), which appears to have outstripped demand. The other main source of visible inventory are the SHFE stocks, which show a near 70,000 tonne reduction so far this year and in early May stood at around 375,000 tonnes. We expect the recent uptrend in Chinese output to continue. Initial estimates from the National Bureau of Statistics suggest that output set a new record high of 1.46m tonnes in April, 6.9% up on a year earlier. ###### **Chinese government tries to rein in capacity** The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) has issued a circular to “curb overcapacity of aluminium smelting and prevent redundant construction of aluminium smelter projects”. There are currently 23 proposed projects with a combined capacity of 7.74 million tonnes per year (tpy). This, in theory, could take Chinese capacity to 30 million tpy by 2015. Last year, output was 17.6 million tonnes and capacity was 22.5 million tpy. They have introduced a number of measures including: provinces should stop providing bank loans for new projects; the removal of preferential energy tariffs and other incentives for aluminium smelters, and the re-submission of new plans for any projects under consideration. ###### **Further gains in Chinese output** Global output of primary aluminium reached a fresh high of 69,800 tonnes per day (tpd) in March, according to the IAI, up from 69,600 tpd in February and 66,000 tpd a year earlier. Cumulative production in the first three months of the year was 6.7% up on the corresponding period of 2010. ###### **Growth beginning to slow outside of China** Although production outside of China is still showing yearon-year gains in excess of 5%, output has levelled out over the last three months. Norsk Hydro’s Qatalum smelter in Qatar, which came on stream in late 2009, is expected to produce around 500,000 tonnes of primary aluminium this year. ###### **Mixed fortunes in the Americas** The impact of the restart of US smelters is clearly shown in the latest Aluminum Association data. US primary output in the first four months of the year was 9.6% higher at 614,605 tonnes, while output in April was 13.6% up yearon year. This uptrend is set to continue. As we noted in the previous issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, Ormet Corporation, has recently restored its aluminium smelter to full capacity that should boost output by 82,000 tonnes this year. Ormet’s total production capacity with six potlines is about 266,000 tpy. Century Aluminium has also ramped up production at its Hannibal smelter, while Alcoa is bringing online idled lines at its Massena East, Wenatchee and Intalco smelters. United States. In terms of China the recent announcement of new measures to curb output are more likely to have an impact on 2012 production rather than on this year. ###### **Positive start for aluminium consumption** Some of the industry were concerned that there might be a reaction to last year’s demand growth of 14.6%. However in most areas this has not proved to be the case. Certainly physical premiums are pointing to firm underlying conditions. Japanese spot premiums in May are trading around contract levels of $113/tonne. Elsewhere in Asia, premiums are holding firm at high levels. In Singapore, premiums are in a range of $85-90/tonne, while in Indonesia and Thailand they are reported to be as high as $120/tonne. Reflecting steady demand in Europe, premiums for duty-paid physical aluminium have improved, with Rotterdam material in the range of $190-210/tonne, up from $185-200/tonne at the end of the first quarter. Meanwhile, premiums for duty-unpaid material are at $130-135/tonne, close to their highest levels since June last year. According to ABAL, the industry organisation, Brazilian output in March was down 8.5% year-on-year at 131,700 tonnes. Output at Votorantim registered a 17.4% decline to 33,200 tonnes due to planned maintenance work. Alcoa’s output was down 6.4% at 29,300 tonnes, largely due to lower output at its Sao Luis smelter. Production at Novelis fell by nearly 50% to 4,100 tonnes, reflecting the permanent closure of its 60,000 tpy Aratu smelter in December last year due to high power and operating costs. In North America, it appear

s that strong demand growth and higher transport costs are supporting higher physical premiums. The latter has played a particularly important role with a severe shortage of trucks; a situation that has been exacerbated by the flooding of the Ohio River which has seen companies use trucks rather than river barges. US Midwest spot premiums rose from $143-154/tonne in March to a range of $200-220/tonne in mid May. ###### **Short-term weakness in Japanese demand...** ###### **Production forecasts are unchanged** According to the IAI, growth in global output in the first quarter was 6.7%.
